verdicts.quote: The readBytes() method reads a 32-bit unsigned integer from the stream as contentLength, then allocates a byte array of size (int)contentLength. The check `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` permits allocation of up to Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 bytes (approximately 2GB).
verdicts.why: F01 is exactly the length-prefix-drives-allocation mechanism: an untrusted 32-bit length field read off the wire is used directly as the size of the byte array, and the array is allocated up front with no check that the stream actually carries that many bytes. The exploit it describes (one small frame claiming a ~2GB field to force the allocation) is the 'buffer created before the payload has been shown to exist' case.

verdicts.quote: The readFieldValue() method (lines 158-221) is called recursively: case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() again; case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray() which calls readFieldValue() again. No recursion depth limit is enforced in the code.
verdicts.why: F02 names the mutual-recursion cycle among the decoding routines (readFieldValue -> readTable/readArray -> readFieldValue) and states that nothing bounds the depth, so nesting depth in the attacker-supplied frame controls call-stack depth until StackOverflowError. That is the described mechanism, not merely a mention of it.
